\boxed{46}

For each positive integer \(k\) the student may erase all occurrences of \(k\), or all occurrences of \(-k\), or none; erasing more of a chosen sign never hurts and never creates a sum \(0\).  So we may assume the student chooses a sign for every absolute value that appears.  Encode this by a Boolean variable \(x_k\) (\(x_k=1\) means erase \(k\), \(x_k=0\) means erase \(-k\)).

Each pair becomes a clause: e.g. \((k,\ell)\) gives \(x_k\lor x_\ell\), \((k,-\ell)\) gives \(x_k\lor\neg x_\ell\), \((-k,-\ell)\) gives \(\neg x_k\lor\neg x_\ell\), and a diagonal pair \((k,k)\) (resp. \((-k,-k)\)) gives the unit clause \(x_k\) (resp. \(\neg x_k\)).  The score is the number of satisfied clauses.  The board condition says no variable has both unit clauses \(x_k\) and \(\neg x_k\).

In any optimal assignment every unit clause is satisfied: if a unit \(x_k\) were false, flipping \(x_k\) would satisfy it and could not unsatisfy anything (no clause was being satisfied by the literal \(x_k\)).  Hence all unsatisfied pairs are binary.

Let \(u\) be the number of unsatisfied pairs.  For a variable \(v\), let \(U_v\) be the number of unsatisfied pairs incident to \(v\) and \(S_v\) the number of satisfied pairs that would become unsatisfied if \(v\) were flipped.  Optimality gives \(U_v\le S_v\).  Summing over all variables,
\[
2u=\sum U_v\le\sum S_v.
\]
Each satisfied binary pair contributes at most \(1\) to \(\sum S_v\) (only when exactly one of its literals satisfies it) and each satisfied unit pair contributes \(1\); thus \(\sum S_v\le 68-u\).  Hence \(2u\le 68-u\), i.e. \(3u\le 68\), so \(u\le 22\).  The student can always score at least \(68-22=46\).

To see \(46\) is best possible, let the board consist of \(23\) copies of \((a,a)\), \(23\) copies of \((b,b)\) and \(22\) copies of \((-a,-b)\).  A legal erasure cannot contain both \(a\) and \(-a\) nor both \(b\) and \(-b\); the best choice (erase \(a\) and \(b\)) scores exactly \(46\).  Therefore \(N=46\).
